question: What force does 'how many' have here?

positions.position: It expresses the abundance of destroyed peoples.
positions.reasons: Al-Samīn says كم must be fronted; al-Ālūsī prefers the exclamatory or informative sense. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls it an exclamatory report.

positions.position: It may be interrogative.
positions.reasons: Al-Ālūsī also reports this reading.

turns_on: Whether كم reports abundance or poses a question.

question: How do 'how many' and 'of a generation' work syntactically?

positions.position: كم is the object of أهلكنا, and من قرن specifies it.
positions.reasons: Al-Nasafī calls من قرن an accusative modifier, noting that قرنا without من would be clearer. Al-Samīn says كم is obligatorily fronted.

positions.position: A people, nation, or civilization of one era relative to successors.
positions.reasons: Al-Kāshifī says a group gathered at one time. Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī relate the term to the projecting or preceding horn. Asad cites 19:98.

question: How long is a qarn said to last?

positions.position: One hundred years.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports this estimate; al-Ālūsī notes disagreement.

positions.position: Eighty years.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports this estimate; al-Ālūsī notes disagreement.

positions.position: Seventy years.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports this estimate; al-Ālūsī notes disagreement.

question: Who are the people compared with the former generations?

positions.position: The boastful unbelievers, especially Quraysh or Mecca's people.
positions.reasons: Muqātil names Mecca's people; Ibn ʿĀshūr says Arab polytheists and an intervening address to the Prophet. Al-Biqāʿī says they saw the earlier peoples' homes and traces.

positions.position: Al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith and his associates.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabrisī says they groomed their hair, wore silk, and boasted of their appearance.

turns_on: Whether the pronoun denotes the unbelievers generally or al-Naḍr's group.

question: What does 'they were better' modify?

positions.position: It is an accusative adjective of كم.
positions.reasons: Al-Zamakhsharī and Abū al-Baqāʾ say أحسن alone would be accusative. Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn object that كم cannot take an adjective.

positions.position: It modifies قرن with plural agreement by collective sense.
positions.reasons: Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn cite the Basran rule on كم. Al-Samīn calls the adjective genitive and cites 54:44 and 36:32; al-Ālūsī says singular agreement is possible.

positions.position: The clause is circumstantial.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī gives this parse.

turns_on: The attachment of the clause and whether كم can be qualified.

question: What does athāth denote?

positions.position: Household furnishings or possessions, often decorative.
positions.reasons: Mujāhid includes adornment; al-Layth speaks of kinds of household goods. Al-Aṣamm includes furniture and clothes. Ibn ʿĀshūr emphasizes decoration. Al-Bint al-Shāṭiʾ argues from Quranic use, especially 16:80, for abundant furnishings as distinct from wider matāʿ. Al-Wāḥidī adduces thick plants and dense hair, with a poem, for the root.

positions.position: Property or wealth broadly, including livestock and slaves in one report.
positions.reasons: Abū Zayd includes livestock, slaves and household goods. Ibn ʿAṭiyya also includes livestock. Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Suddī and Qatāda give wealth. Asad stresses abundance; al-Bint al-Shāṭiʾ disputes the breadth as usual usage.

positions.position: Clothing or things worn and spread out.
positions.reasons: Muqātil and al-Ḥasan say clothing; al-Harawī restricts it to worn and spread things.

positions.position: Rugs, carpets, or fine bedding.
positions.reasons: ʿAṭāʾ from Ibn ʿAbbās says rugs and carpets; al-Kashshāf fine bedding; al-Nasafī new carpets.

positions.position: New or fine furnishings, contrasted with worn khirthī.
positions.reasons: Al-Kashshāf, al-Qurṭubī and al-Ālūsī cite al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī al-Ṭūsī's poem about worn goods. Al-Bayḍāwī allows the restriction.

positions.position: Appearance or bearing.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAbbās is reported with this gloss; the paired Muqātil gloss is clothing.

positions.position: Unseen or useful goods paired with visible ornaments or blessings.
positions.reasons: Al-Māwardī reports several paired explanations: new clothing and blessings, unseen and visible possessions, wealth and appearance, useful goods and ornaments.

turns_on: Whether the word is general property, household goods, a particular kind of good, or appearance.

positions.position: It is a collective without a singular of the same form.
positions.reasons: Al-Farrāʾ compares matāʿ and gives alternate plural forms ātha and athat. Some lexicographers say it denotes a large quantity. Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Ṭabarī, al-Jishumī and al-Bint al-Shāṭiʾ transmit the view.

positions.position: It has singular athātha.
positions.reasons: Al-Aḥmar compares ḥamām/ḥamāma and saḥāb; Abū Zayd and al-Aṣamm also provide a singular.

question: What does the final word mean?

positions.position: Visible appearance, beauty, form, dress or display of goods.
positions.reasons: Mujāhid says what people see. Ibn ʿAbbās specifies color and beauty; al-Ḥasan forms. Al-Ṭabarī cites ʿAlqama's poem for displayed goods, explaining ṣawwān as a clothes chest. Al-Jawharī and Abū ʿUbayda cite poetry for conspicuous dress. Al-Fārisī distinguishes the thing seen from raʾy and ruʾya and compares 3:13. Al-Bint al-Shāṭiʾ includes witnessed or imagined scenes and rereads the disputed poem accordingly.

positions.position: Watered luxuriance, freshness, or fullness visible in appearance.
positions.reasons: Yaḥyā links rain with crops and livestock. Al-Naḥḥās describes skin replete with blessing. Abū ʿAlī treats rayy as verbal noun or passive participle. Mundhir reports a view that their lands were well irrigated and abundant.

positions.position: Fine attire or gathered adornments under the zāy reading.
positions.reasons: Al-Farrāʾ cites zayyaytu al-jāriya. Ibn Jinnī derives ziyy from zawaytu, citing the Prophet's 'earth gathered' expression and al-Aʿshā's poetry. Al-Qurṭubī repeats the expression; al-Ālūsī cites a poem on attractive furnishings.

positions.position: Wealth, standing and residence.
positions.reasons: Al-Ḥasan is reported to say wealth; Qatāda adds standing and residence.

positions.position: Good judgment concerning property.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabarī reports this derivation from rawiya for unhamzated riyyan.

positions.position: Drink or satiation.
positions.reasons: The Ibn al-Azraq exchange and al-Itqān cite a poem; al-Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says the sense is outside the seven canonical readings, lacks Arabic support, and the poem is better read as appearance.

positions.position: Mutual display of beauty.
positions.reasons: Al-Yazīdī's riyāʾ is derived from showing off to one another.

turns_on: The proposed roots of sight, watering, adornment, judgment, drink or display.

question: How is the final word read?

positions.position: Riʾyan with hamza before yāʾ.
positions.reasons: Ibn Mujāhid names Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī; Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir vary. Kufans and Abū ʿAmr preserve raʾaytu. Al-Ṭabarī prefers the sight derivation by consensus of interpreters. Ibn al-Jazarī explains omission of hamza's image in the script by adjacent y-shaped letters, rejecting explanation from kasra alone. Al-Samīn says Abū ʿAmr avoids confusion with rayy.

positions.position: Riyyan with doubled yāʾ and no hamza.
positions.reasons: Medinan readers and transmissions of Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir use it. Hamza may become yāʾ after kasra and assimilate, or rayy may mean watered prosperity. Al-Naḥḥās favors agreement with unhamzated endings; al-Ṭabarī accepts it with the sight meaning. The second canonical reading keeps that root and sense.

positions.position: A light single-yāʾ form without hamza.
positions.reasons: Ṭalḥa and a report from Ibn ʿAbbās transmit it. Ibn Jinnī proposes dropping a yāʾ or moving hamza's vowel before deleting it. Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī defend it; al-Naḥḥās, Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Qurṭubī suspect error or weakness. Al-Rāzī reports deletion of hamza from ريئا after shifting its vowel to the preceding yāʾ.

positions.position: Riyʾan with yāʾ before final hamza.
positions.reasons: Abū Bakr via ʿĀṣim and Ḥumayd transmit it. Al-Zajjāj deems it linguistically possible though unreported to him. Kathīr's rāʾanī and another poem witness inversion; Sībawayh attests rāʾ. Al-Samīn doubts metathesis but allows derivation from rāʾahu yarāhu.

positions.position: Ziyyan or zayyan with zāy.
positions.reasons: Ubayy, Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Yazīd al-Barbarī, al-Aʿṣam and others are named. It means appearance, dress or gathered adornment. Al-Ṭabarī rejects its departure from the reciters' reading but accepts the interpretation.

positions.position: Riyāʾ from mutual display.
positions.reasons: Al-Yazīdī transmits it; al-Samīn says its first hamza is eased to yāʾ.

turns_on: The consonants, placement of hamza and derivation differ.

question: How is Hamza's hamza treated at pause?

positions.position: Replace hamza with yāʾ and articulate both yāʾs clearly.
positions.reasons: Al-Kāfī and al-Tabṣira prefer this; al-Tabṣira calls it established. Ibn al-Jazarī prefers it as analogical and common. For related ruʾyā readers agree on wāw substitution after ḍamma.

positions.position: Replace hamza with yāʾ and assimilate.
positions.reasons: Al-Tadhkira and al-Dānī prefer explicit transmission from Ḥamza and agreement with the script; al-ʿUnwān gives only this. Al-Taysīr and al-Shāṭibī give both. Al-Hudhalī and others allow related Abū Jaʿfar assimilation in ruʾyā, while Ibn Shurayḥ weakens it.

positions.position: Realize hamza fully to prevent a meaning change.
positions.reasons: Al-Tadhkira proposes this; Ibn al-Jazarī rejects it as against transmitted performance.

positions.position: Delete hamza and stop on one light yāʾ.
positions.reasons: Al-Fārisī reports this from the script; Ibn al-Jazarī deems it invalid and impermissible.

turns_on: Whether transmission, analogy, script or possible confusion with rayy governs the pause.

question: What happened to the earlier peoples and their advantages?

positions.position: Many earlier peoples had better goods and looks, yet God destroyed them and their resources.
positions.reasons: Muqātil says wealth and bodies were destroyed; al-Ṭabarī says property was destroyed and appearance changed; Qatāda adds standing and residence before disfigurement. Al-Biqāʿī says unprefixed 'before' spans all earlier generations and their visible traces. Ibn ʿĀshūr frames an address to the Prophet.

question: What lesson or warning follows from their destruction?

positions.position: Wealth, beauty and status neither establish divine favor nor protect deniers from punishment.
positions.reasons: Al-Rāzī also rejects the inference that God's beloved cannot suffer grief. Al-Jishumī extends the lesson to leadership at Resurrection. Al-Qurṭubī allows punishment here or later. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī contrasts short worldly life with eternity. Al-Kāshifī's couplet gives the lesson. Kuranyolu names ʿĀd and Thamūd, their cultivation and thriving countries. Study Quran cites destruction parallels at 6:6, 7:4, 17:17, 19:98, 21:11, 22:45, 28:58, 38:3, 44:37, 47:13 and 50:36.

question: How does the verse answer the previous boast and connect to other verses?

positions.position: It rebuts the 19:73 boast of superior station and company by recalling peoples with greater worldly advantages.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī compares Pharaoh's Egyptian kingdom and rivers in 43:51–55, then his drowning. Ibn al-Jawzī and Abū Ḥayyān connect 6:6 and 16:80. Study Quran cites further destruction parallels; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the threat interrupts before the reply.

positions.position: Seekers humble and discipline themselves; love of wealth, status and desire ruined earlier deniers.
positions.reasons: Al-Bursawī transmits the Najmī taʾwīl contrasting disciplined seekers with indulgent deniers.
